title: The Coin Shop
strapline: Real coins, a real till, and the maths of 'have I got enough?'
intent: Children meet money as a real tool — coins that look different, are worth different amounts, and buy things.
Children count out coins one by one and begin to see that money is about quantity, not just objects.
Children solve genuine problems: what does it cost, have I got enough, how much change is left.
Children rehearse the social script of shopping — asking, paying, thanking — full of rich back-and-forth talk.
Children start to recognise coins by name and feel and to sort them by their differences.
implementation: Set up a small shop with real coins (cleaned) or good replica coins, a working till or cash box, and a few items priced at 1p, 2p, 5p.
Keep prices low and whole at first — everything 'one coin' — then let costs grow as children's counting grows.
Model the whole exchange slowly: 'that's three pennies please — one, two, three — thank you, here's your change.'
Wonder aloud about enough and not enough: 'the apple is 5p and I've got 4p — oh no, what shall I do?'
Put out price labels, a notepad for the shopkeeper's takings, and a purse each so counting coins is unavoidable.
Rotate the stock to match interests — a cake shop, a garden centre, a toy stall — so the shop stays alive.
Sit in as a customer sometimes and make deliberate mistakes for the shopkeeper to spot and correct.
key_questions: How many pennies do you need to pay for that?
Have you got enough — how can we check?
Which coin is worth more, do you think?
If it costs 5p and you give me 6p, what should I give you back?
How much money is in the till now?

impact.text: Children count coins accurately, one number word per coin.
Children recognise and name some coins and sort them by their differences.
Children work out 'have I got enough?' and solve simple money problems.
Children use the language of shopping — cost, pay, change, more, less.
Children take on roles, take turns and negotiate as shopkeeper and customer.
Children keep going to sort out a tricky bit of change until it works.

enhancements: Purses and wallets, and a coin sorter or tray to organise the till.
Price tags children can write themselves, and a 'special offer' sign.
A set of coin-rubbing plates and crayons to explore what's on each coin.
A weighing scale so items can be sold 'by the bag' — five conkers for 5p.
A cash-machine box that dispenses a set number of coins.
Receipts and a takings book so the shopkeeper records each sale.

playing_exploring: Children step into the shopkeeper role and drive the play themselves.
Real coins hold a fascination that pulls the counting along.
active_learning: Children persist to count out the exact money and get the change right.
Running the shop gives them a goal — a full till — worth working towards.
creating_thinking: Children plan what to buy against what they have, and adjust when it's not enough.
They invent prices, offers and rules, thinking flexibly about value.
